conceptual assets.information: The 32-bit words written for transmission to the LED are serialized into the neooled output; correct IP use depends on preserving and transmitting these words.
conceptual assets.rubric reason: The payload may be sensitive before transmission and is exposed through the neooled_o output after the FIFO and serial engine process it (lines 192, 239, 257-270, 318). A bus write supplies the transmitted word and the loaded or shifted value controls the output waveform, so alteration can corrupt the LED data (lines 191-192, 239, 257-270).
conceptual assets.attack: An attacker could observe the serialized neooled_o signal or alter bus write data to disclose or corrupt the LED payload.

conceptual assets.information: The enable state activates the LED engine and external clock generation, and controls whether queued data is cleared or the serial engine progresses.
conceptual assets.rubric reason: The enable bit is writable through a bus control write and directly controls the externally visible clock enable and engine behavior (lines 130, 160, 193, 231). Clearing or changing the enable can disable the clock, clear queued data, and prevent serial transfers from operating (lines 160, 193, 231).
conceptual assets.attack: An attacker could overwrite the enable control to disable the clock output, clear queued data, and stop LED transfers.

conceptual assets.information: The mode and strobe settings select how each queued word is interpreted and whether the serial engine performs the normal data or strobe sequence.
conceptual assets.rubric reason: Bus writes modify the mode and strobe settings, which select the serial mode, bit count, and subsequent engine state, so unauthorized modification can produce an incorrect LED protocol sequence (lines 131-132, 240-252, 260-271).
conceptual assets.attack: An attacker could change the mode or strobe controls so transmitted words use the wrong encoding or sequence.

conceptual assets.information: The clock prescaler and total, zero-bit, and one-bit timing values define the rate and pulse widths of the LED waveform; correct serial timing depends on them.
conceptual assets.rubric reason: The timing settings are writable configuration state and determine the sampled clock, pulse widths, and transfer completion timing (lines 133, 135-137, 225, 261-263, 285-299). A modified prescaler can select a non-toggling clock-generator bit and prevent progress, while modified timing values can delay or prevent completion or produce an invalid waveform (lines 225, 278-299).
conceptual assets.attack: An attacker could program an unsuitable prescaler or pulse limit to stall the serial engine or make the LED waveform invalid.

conceptual assets.information: The interrupt request reports that the enabled transmitter has reached its configured FIFO service condition, allowing software or another module to service queued LED data.
conceptual assets.rubric reason: The interrupt output is produced from the engine enable and FIFO availability conditions and can therefore be made incorrect by altered control or queue state (lines 201-203).
conceptual assets.attack: An attacker could manipulate the control or transmitted-data conditions so irq_o is falsely asserted or suppressed, causing the host to service the transmitter incorrectly.

considered, not kept.reason: ctrl.irq_conf only tunes the interrupt-request output, so the Port options rule excludes it as a piece of its own (lines 134, 202-203).
The request strobe, direction, and address are access command fields that select or qualify writes and reads rather than information of their own (lines 127-139, 191).
The state, counters, busy indication, and done pulse only order or time the LED transfer and are excluded by the Sequencing state and Pacing pulses rules (lines 215-223, 232-313, 321).

clk_i, rstn_i, and the clock-generator sampling path are clocks, resets, or pacing signals rather than conceptual information under the Clocks and resets and Pacing pulses rules (lines 109-121, 212-225, 278-299).
The acknowledge repeats the request strobe and the error response is constant, so the Bus handshake copies rule bars them as information of their own (lines 123-124).

The response data word is only a merge of individual configuration and status values; the underlying kept settings and output status, not the aggregate word, are the separate information pieces (lines 140-153).
FIFO_DEPTH only fixes the implementation and reported capacity at build time and cannot be changed or withheld at run time (lines 20, 145, 167-171).
